title: Songs of mourning
hookLine: Guru Nanak's dirges are sung for the dead, remembering that all must go (Vadhans M1, ang 578)

cards: In old Punjab, when someone died, the women of the village gathered in the courtyard. They sat in a circle and wailed, a lament with a rhythm to it, one woman leading, the others answering, beating their chests.
The custom was called siapa, and the lament songs were alaahnees. Grief was loud, public, and shaped by tradition. Guru Nanak knew those songs.
And he did something unexpected with them: he wrote his own.

teach.b: Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa, his laments, are in Raag Vadhans, starting on Ang five seventy-eight. He kept the form people knew, but changed what it sang about.
The first begins, in paraphrase: blessed is the Creator, the true King, who has set the whole world to its tasks. When the measure of a life is full, the soul is taken, and loved ones cry out.
The body and soul are parted when the days are done. Notice the first word.

teach.h: A DIRGE THAT OPENS WITH BLESSED.
teach.b: A mourning song that opens with blessed. It doesn't deny the grief; the hymn says plainly that the family weeps. But it sets the grief inside something larger: a Creator who gives each life its span.
Then the truth that runs through these songs: everyone who comes must go. It isn't said to scold anyone for crying. It's said the way a friend at a funeral says, gently, this is the road we all walk.
Sikh practice took this to heart: the Sikh code of conduct discourages loud wailing at a death. Kirtan is sung, often Kirtan Sohila, the bedtime prayer, and the Ardas is said.
A reading of the Guru Granth Sahib is often begun in the days after, and the alaahneeaa are among the hymns sung.
But it's held in praise, and in the plain, shared knowledge that this is how every life goes.

how: At Sikh funerals and in the days after, families gather for kirtan, Kirtan Sohila and Ardas, and Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa are among the hymns sung, in place of the old custom of ritual wailing.

a wedding song sung by women
a lament, a song of mourning

games.q: songs of mourning — tap the pairs.
p: the old custom of ritual wailing

s: Guru Nanak's laments say the family shouldn't weep
the hymn says plainly that loved ones cry; it holds the grief in praise.
the first lament opens by praising the Creator
blessed is the Creator, the true King, who set the world to its tasks.

games.q: you're writing a mourning song in a land where laments are loud and ritual wailing is the custom. what does Guru Nanak do?
o: keeps the lament's form, and fills it with praise and the truth that all must go.
games.why: he wrote his own alaahneeaa: the familiar form, opening with blessed is the Creator.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has died, a grandparent, a friend, even a pet, and let an ordinary memory come rather than the hardest one: their laugh, a meal, a phrase they used.
Let any sadness be there too, and quietly give thanks for the days they were given. If you pray, say Waheguru for them.

wordCard.voice: Alaahnee. A lament, the old Punjabi mourning song. Guru Nanak's alaahneeaa keep its form but open with praise, and remember that everyone who comes must go.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: laments; the heading of Guru Nanak's mourning songs in Raag Vadhans.

carryVoice: Your line: all must go. Grief is allowed here, and it is held in praise. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Vadhans Mahalla 1, Alaahneeaa (dhan sirandaa sachaa paatisaahu), Ang 578
